# Introduction

`r Biocpkg("exposomeSC")` relates exposures measured on donors to gene
expression within the annotated cell types of single-cell RNA-seq data. Its
container, the `SingleCellExposomeExperiment`, keeps a donor-level exposure
table next to the cells of a `SingleCellExperiment` and checks that the two
agree. Its main analysis, `run_sc_exwas()`, sums the raw counts of each cell
type within each donor and fits a model in which the donors, not the cells, are
the replicates.

Cells of one donor share that donor's exposure, so they are not independent
observations of it; a test that treats them as such is too confident
[@squair2021]. The quantity that `run_sc_exwas()` estimates is the log2 fold
change of a gene's expression rate within a cell type per unit of the exposure.
A change in the number of cells of a type is a different quantity and has a
function of its own (Section \@ref(composition)).

The package works with the classes of Bioconductor. The container extends
`SingleCellExperiment`, the pseudobulk counts are `SummarizedExperiment`
objects, and the results are `DataFrame`s; those of `run_sc_exwas()` carry the
settings of the run in their `metadata()`. The models are fitted by
`r Biocpkg("edgeR")`,
`r Biocpkg("DESeq2")` and `r Biocpkg("limma")`. In a workflow the package comes
after quality control and the annotation of cell types, which it takes as
given: its input is a `SingleCellExperiment` with raw counts, a column that
names the donor of each cell and a column with the cell type.

Every association the package estimates is observational. Exposures such as
smoking are not assigned at random, and nothing in the package identifies a
causal effect.

The vignette uses the two data sets that the package ships. Both are real and
both are small on purpose: they show what the functions take and what they
return, and they are far too small to support conclusions. The first, 352
airway epithelial cells of 12 donors, serves Sections \@ref(data) to
\@ref(composition). The second, 1,032 blood cells of 43 patients with measured
plasma compounds and surface proteins, serves Section \@ref(incov).

Some sections use packages that exposomeSC only suggests:
`r CRANpkg("lme4")`, `r CRANpkg("lmerTest")` and `r CRANpkg("pbkrtest")`,
`r CRANpkg("mgcv")`,
`r CRANpkg("qgcomp")`, `r CRANpkg("metafor")`, `r CRANpkg("ppcor")`,
`r Biocpkg("variancePartition")` and `r Biocpkg("fgsea")`. A chunk that needs
one of them is run when it is installed. Two further vignettes cover the
cross-omic networks and checks of a result by permutation.

# Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("exposomeSC")
```

# The airway data {#data}

```{r load, message=FALSE}
library(exposomeSC)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
x <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "hlca_airway_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
x
```

The object holds the raw counts of 352 tracheal epithelial cells of the Human
Lung Cell Atlas core [@sikkema2023], from its study of smokers and never
smokers [@goldfarbmuren2020]: six heavy smokers, with at least 15 pack-years,
and six never smokers, with up to 10 basal, 10 secretory and 10
multiciliated-lineage cells per donor. `?hlca_airway_subset` describes the
selection, and the script that made the file from the public H5AD is installed
with the package (`system.file("scripts", package = "exposomeSC")`). The atlas
is distributed under the CC BY 4.0 licence, and the object carries its
provenance:

```{r provenance}
metadata(x)$source[c("data", "dataset_version", "licence", "references")]
table(x$donor_id, x$cell_type)
```

The donor-level variables are the exposure data of the object, one row per
donor, with a description of each variable. `sampleColumn()` names the column
of `colData()` that assigns the cells to the donors.

```{r accessors}
exposureData(x)
exposureInfo(x)
exposureVariables(x)
sampleColumn(x)
head(cellSampleMap(x), 3)
```

`build_scee()` makes such an object from a `SingleCellExperiment` and a numeric
matrix with one row per donor. It stops when a donor of the cells has no row in
the matrix or a row has no cells. Here the object is taken apart and built
again:

```{r build}
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = counts(x)),
    colData = colData(x),
    rowData = rowData(x)
)
rebuilt <- build_scee(sce, exposureData(x), sample_col = "donor_id",
    exposure_info = exposureInfo(x))
identical(exposureData(rebuilt), exposureData(x))
```

Donor variables often arrive as columns of the cell annotations, with the value
of a donor repeated for each of its cells, as in the metadata of a Seurat
object. `seurat_to_exposure()` reduces such columns to the matrix that
`build_scee()` takes:

```{r cell-table}
cell_table <- data.frame(donor_id = x$donor_id,
    exposureData(x)[x$donor_id, ], row.names = colnames(x))
head(cell_table, 3)
donor_table <- seurat_to_exposure(cell_table, sample_col = "donor_id",
    exposure_cols = exposureVariables(x))
identical(donor_table, exposureData(x))
```

`donor_pseudobulk()` returns the counts that `run_sc_exwas()` fits its models
to: one `SummarizedExperiment` per cell type, with one column per donor and the
exposure data as column data. Looking at them is the first check of any result.
The counts of *CYP1B1* in basal cells, a gene that returns below, are:

```{r pseudobulk}
pseudobulk <- donor_pseudobulk(x)
pseudobulk
basal <- pseudobulk[["Basal"]]
cyp1b1 <- rownames(x)[rowData(x)$symbol == "CYP1B1"]
data.frame(
    smoking = basal$smoking,
    CYP1B1 = assay(basal, "counts")[cyp1b1, ],
    all_genes = colSums(assay(basal, "counts"))
)
```

# The association model {#exwas}

`run_sc_exwas()` fits, for each cell type, a donor-level model of the
pseudobulk counts on the exposure and the covariates. The default backend is
the quasi-likelihood model of `r Biocpkg("edgeR")` [@chen2025]. Here the
exposure is smoking, adjusted for the 10x chemistry, which differs between
donors:

```{r exwas}
fit <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking", covariates = "chemistry_v3")
dim(fit)
top <- head(fit, 8)
top$symbol <- rowData(x)[top$gene, "symbol"]
top[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "statistic", "pvalue", "padj",
    "padj_global", "n_donors")]
```

The result has one row per tested gene and cell type, ordered by `padj_global`.
`padj` is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment within a cell type and
`padj_global` the adjustment across all tested gene-by-cell-type pairs. For the
edgeR backend `se` is `NA`: the quasi-likelihood F test gives no standard error
of the coefficient, and `statistic` is the square root of the F statistic with
the sign of the log fold change. The settings and what was done in each cell
type are kept with the result:

```{r exwas-metadata}
parameters <- metadata(fit)$parameters
parameters[c("method", "se_method", "statistic_type")]
diagnostics <- metadata(fit)$diagnostics
vapply(diagnostics, function(d) d$n_donors, numeric(1))
vapply(diagnostics, function(d) d$n_genes_tested, numeric(1))
```

One donor has only two multiciliated-lineage cells, fewer than `min_cells`, so
that cell type is fitted with 11 donors.

These numbers must not be read as findings. With six donors per group and at
most ten cells per donor and cell type, a few counts decide a result: the table
of Section \@ref(data) shows that *CYP1B1* has no count in the basal cells of
the never smokers and between 1 and 18 in those of a smoker, and the size of
such an estimate depends on little. The same model on larger sets of cells of
the same donors, which were analysed when the data set was made, gave other
lists of genes below a threshold.

# Other models for the same question

## Other backends

`method = "voom_dream"` fits the voom model of `r Biocpkg("limma")` through
`r Biocpkg("variancePartition")` [@hoffman2021], and `method = "DESeq2"` a Wald
test of `r Biocpkg("DESeq2")`. Both return a standard error of the
coefficient. The columns are the same for every backend.

```{r voom, eval=has("variancePartition")}
fit_voom <- run_sc_exwas(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", method = "voom_dream", celltypes = "Basal")
fit_voom$symbol <- rowData(x)[fit_voom$gene, "symbol"]
head(fit_voom[, c("symbol", "log2FC", "se", "statistic", "pvalue")], 3)
```

## A negative binomial model with an offset

`run_sc_exwas_pb_offset()` fits a negative binomial model of each pseudobulk
count with the logarithm of the donor's total count as offset [@lee2024], for
the genes named in `target_genes`, here three. Its p-values are Wald tests and
can be too small with few donors. It has no `padj` within a cell type;
`padj_global` is adjusted across the tests that were made. It also has no
`min_cells`: every donor with a cell of the type enters the model, the donor
with two multiciliated-lineage cells included.

```{r offset}
genes <- rownames(x)[match(c("ALDH3A1", "NQO1", "GPX2"), rowData(x)$symbol)]
offset_fit <- run_sc_exwas_pb_offset(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", target_genes = genes)
offset_fit$symbol <- rowData(x)[offset_fit$gene, "symbol"]
offset_fit[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "se", "statistic", "pvalue",
    "padj_global")]
```

## A mixed model of the cells

`run_sc_exwas_glmm()` keeps the cells as observations. For each gene it fits a
linear mixed model of the log-normalised expression of the cells, with random
intercepts for the donor and for the donor within a cell type, and tests the
effect of the exposure in each cell type with denominator degrees of freedom
by the method of Satterthwaite, the default, or of Kenward and Roger, which
its help page advises for fewer than about 30 donors and which is used here.
It is much slower than the pseudobulk models, so it is meant for a few genes.

```{r glmm, eval=has("lme4", "lmerTest", "pbkrtest")}
mixed_fit <- run_sc_exwas_glmm(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", target_genes = genes,
    ddf = "Kenward-Roger")
mixed_fit$symbol <- rowData(x)[mixed_fit$gene, "symbol"]
mixed_fit[, c("symbol", "celltype", "log2FC", "se", "df", "pvalue",
    "padj_global")]
```

The response is log2(counts per 10,000 + 1) of each cell, so the coefficient,
although the column is called `log2FC`, is not on the scale of the pseudobulk
estimates. `family = "nbinom"` fits a negative binomial mixed model with a
likelihood-ratio test for each gene and cell type instead; that takes minutes
for a few genes even on these data and is not run here.

# More than one exposure, and differences between cell types

`run_multi_exwas()` runs the model for several exposures and adds `padj_all`,
the adjustment across all exposures and cell types. Age is used here as a
second donor variable; `celltypes` restricts the run to basal cells.

```{r multi}
both <- run_multi_exwas(x, exposures = c("smoking", "age"),
    covariates = "chemistry_v3", celltypes = "Basal")
table(both$exposure)
both$symbol <- rowData(x)[both$gene, "symbol"]
head(both[, c("symbol", "exposure", "log2FC", "pvalue", "padj_global",
    "padj_all")], 3)
```

A small p-value in one cell type and a large one in another do not show that
the effect differs between the two [@gelman2006]. `run_interaction_test()`
tests the difference itself, for the genes in `target_genes` or, by default,
for the 50 most variable genes:

```{r interaction}
interaction <- run_interaction_test(x, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3")
interaction$symbol <- rowData(x)[interaction$gene, "symbol"]
head(interaction[order(interaction$p_interaction),
    c("symbol", "p_interaction", "padj_interaction", "n_celltypes",
        "n_donors")], 3)
```

# Gene sets

`run_gsea()` ranks the genes of each cell type by the test statistic and runs
`r Biocpkg("fgsea")` on the ranking. Gene sets are named lists of gene
identifiers as in the row names of the object. The three sets below are short
lists written for this example, not a curated collection; they are mapped from
symbols to the Ensembl identifiers of the data.

```{r gene-sets}
symbols <- list(
    xenobiotic_response = c("CYP1B1", "CYP1A1", "AHRR", "ALDH3A1", "NQO1",
        "AKR1C1", "AKR1C2", "AKR1B10", "GPX2", "TXNRD1", "CBR1", "UGT1A6"),
    cilia = c("FOXJ1", "DNAH5", "DNAI1", "CCDC39", "CCDC40", "RSPH1",
        "TEKT1", "DNAH9", "CFAP43", "SPAG6"),
    secretory = c("MUC5AC", "MUC5B", "SCGB1A1", "TFF3", "BPIFB1", "AGR2",
        "SPDEF", "FOXA3")
)
gene_sets <- lapply(symbols, function(set) {
    rownames(x)[rowData(x)$symbol %in% set]
})
lengths(gene_sets)
```

```{r gsea, eval=has("fgsea")}
set.seed(1)
enrichment <- run_gsea(fit, gene_sets = gene_sets, min_size = 5L)
enrichment[, c("pathway", "celltype", "NES", "pval", "padj_global", "size")]
```

`size` is the number of genes of a set that were tested in the cell type. A set
with fewer than `min_size` of them is left out for that cell type.

# Combining cohorts

`run_meta_exwas()` combines the estimates of independent cohorts by
inverse-variance weighting. It needs results with standard errors, so results
of the edgeR backend are refused, and its random-effects synthesis
(`method = "random"`) needs at least three cohorts. The airway data are one
study; to show the function, the four donors measured with the 10x v2 chemistry
and the eight measured with v3 are treated as two cohorts, each with too few
donors for an analysis of its own, and the genes of the sets above are
combined.

```{r meta, eval=has("variancePartition")}
v3 <- rownames(exposureData(x))[exposureData(x)[, "chemistry_v3"] == 1]
cohorts <- list(
    v2 = x[, !x$donor_id %in% v3],
    v3 = x[, x$donor_id %in% v3]
)
cohort_fits <- lapply(cohorts, function(cohort) {
    cohort_fit <- run_sc_exwas(cohort, exposure = "smoking",
        method = "voom_dream", celltypes = "Basal", min_donors = 4L)
    cohort_fit[cohort_fit$gene %in% unlist(gene_sets), ]
})
meta <- run_meta_exwas(cohort_fits, cohort_names = names(cohort_fits))
meta$symbol <- rowData(x)[meta$gene, "symbol"]
head(meta[order(meta$meta_pvalue), c("symbol", "meta_effect", "meta_se",
    "meta_pvalue", "n_cohorts", "direction")], 3)
```

Subsetting the columns of the object keeps the exposure data of the remaining
donors. The combination treats the standard error of each cohort as known.
With two donors against two in one cohort and four against four in the other
they are anything but, so the p-values of this table show how the function is
called and nothing about the genes.

# Cell composition {#composition}

`run_exposure_composition()` asks whether the proportions of the cell types
differ with the exposure, with the donors as the units. The cells of the airway
data were drawn in equal numbers per donor and cell type, so they carry no
information about composition. The provenance record of the object holds the
numbers of cells of each donor and cell type in the atlas from which they were
drawn, and an object with one label per cell and no counts is enough for the
function:

```{r composition}
eligible <- metadata(x)$source$eligible_cells
eligible
cells <- paste0("cell", seq_len(sum(eligible)))
labels <- DataFrame(
    donor_id = rep(rownames(eligible)[row(eligible)], eligible),
    cell_type = rep(colnames(eligible)[col(eligible)], eligible),
    row.names = cells
)
no_counts <- matrix(0, 0, length(cells), dimnames = list(NULL, cells))
atlas_cells <- build_scee(
    SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = no_counts), colData = labels),
    exposureData(x), sample_col = "donor_id"
)
composition <- run_exposure_composition(atlas_cells, exposure = "smoking",
    covariates = "chemistry_v3")
composition[, c("log2_ratio_change", "se", "pvalue", "padj",
    "median_observed_proportion")]
```

`log2_ratio_change` is the coefficient of the exposure for the log2 ratio of a
cell type to the geometric mean of the others, with a
heteroscedasticity-consistent standard error, and `padj` is the Holm adjustment
over the cell types. A test of the composition as a whole is in
`metadata(composition)$omnibus`. The ratios are among these three cell types as
they were captured; they say nothing about absolute numbers of cells in the
tissue.

# A cohort with measured exposures and proteins {#incov}

The airway data have a smoking status and no measurement of what the donors
were exposed to. The second data set of the package has such measurements:
1,032 blood cells of 43 patients of the INCOV cohort [@su2020], 14 monocytes
and 10 T cells each, with the counts of 192 antibodies for the same cells,
four of them isotype controls, and the plasma levels of 13 compounds of
exogenous origin among the donor variables. All donors had COVID-19 and were
not in hospital when the blood was drawn. `?incov_pbmc_subset` gives the
sources, their licences and every step from the public files to the object.

```{r incov}
y <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "incov_pbmc_subset.rds",
    package = "exposomeSC"))
y
table(y$cell_type)
as.data.frame(exposureInfo(y)[, c("exposure", "family", "source_name")])
```

## Compounds without a value

The plasma levels are relative abundances from untargeted mass spectrometry,
scaled by the authors so that the median of a compound within a batch is 1.
For some donors the table has no value of a compound:

```{r missing-values}
colSums(is.na(exposureData(y)[, c("caffeine", "paraxanthine", "theobromine",
    "pfos", "pfoa", "saccharin")]))
```

The table does not say why a value is missing. In such measurements the usual
reason is that the compound was not detected, but it is not the only one, and
the data can speak against it. Paraxanthine is the main metabolite of
caffeine:

```{r caffeine}
pair <- exposureData(y)[, c("caffeine", "paraxanthine")]
round(pair[!complete.cases(pair), ], 2)
```

The donors without a value of caffeine have little paraxanthine, which fits
caffeine that was not detected. The donors without a value of paraxanthine
have caffeine well above the median of their batch, which is 1; their
paraxanthine is unlikely to have been below detection, so paraxanthine is left
out of what follows.

`exposure_impute_lod()` replaces values below a limit of detection (LOD), by
substitution, by regression on order statistics (`"ros"`) or by multiple
imputation (`"multiple"`). `censored` marks the values that were below the
limit; a missing value that is not marked stays missing.

Three things are assumed here to show the function, and none is in the
source. The section takes every missing value of the five compounds below to
be a compound that was not detected. The table reports no limits of detection;
the smallest value of a compound among all samples of the study, kept in
`exposureInfo(y)$lowest_reported`, stands in for the limit, although the
values were scaled batch by batch and one limit for all batches is itself an
approximation. And `"ros"` takes the logarithms of the levels to be normally
distributed.

```{r compounds}
compounds <- c("caffeine", "theobromine", "pfos", "pfoa", "saccharin")
reported <- exposureData(y)[, compounds]
```

```{r lod}
info <- exposureInfo(y)
lowest <- setNames(info$lowest_reported, info$exposure)[compounds]
signif(lowest, 2)
filled <- exposure_impute_lod(reported, lod = lowest, method = "ros",
    censored = is.na(reported))
attr(filled, "lod_summary")
fill_over_limit <- function(compound) {
    gone <- is.na(reported[, compound])
    round(sort(filled[gone, compound]) / lowest[[compound]], 3)
}
fill_over_limit("caffeine")
fill_over_limit("saccharin")
```

`"ros"` gives one filled-in value for each missing one. The fills follow the
distribution fitted to the reported values and say nothing about which donor
had the larger level, which suits a summary and not an association. With a
limit as low as the one assumed here, the three fills of caffeine all lie just
below it, and only saccharin, with 16 missing values, gets a spread of them.
For an association analysis `?exposure_impute_lod` advises
`method = "multiple"`, which returns several filled-in data sets to analyse
one by one and combine; the sections below use the single `"ros"` fill all the
same, to stay short.

The logarithms of the filled levels replace the reported levels in the object;
`exposureData<-` checks that the donors still agree with the cells, and
`exposureInfo<-` records what the values now are.

```{r replace}
levels <- exposureData(y)
levels[, compounds] <- log2(filled)
exposureData(y) <- levels
round(head(exposureData(y)[, compounds], 3), 2)
info$unit[match(compounds, info$exposure)] <-
    "log2 of the relative abundance, missing values filled in"
exposureInfo(y) <- info
unique(exposureInfo(y)$unit)
```

## Dose and response

`run_dose_response()` compares polynomial models of a gene's pseudobulk
expression on a continuous exposure within one cell type, and
`run_dose_response_gam()` fits a smooth curve with `r CRANpkg("mgcv")`. The
dose here is the plasma level of caffeine, and the genes are 12
interferon-stimulated genes with counts in most donors, which serve as the
outcome in the rest of this section because the donors had a viral infection.

```{r dose}
interferon <- c("IFI6", "ISG15", "MX1", "IFITM3", "STAT1", "XAF1", "EPSTI1",
    "LY6E", "IRF7", "ISG20", "MX2", "EIF2AK2")
dose <- run_dose_response(y, exposure = "caffeine", celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon)
head(dose[order(dose$p_nonlinear), c("gene", "best_model", "linear_coef",
    "p_nonlinear", "n_donors")], 4)
```

`best_model` is the polynomial with the lowest AIC, and `p_nonlinear` an F test
of the cubic against the linear model; it is not adjusted for the number of
genes.

```{r gam, eval=has("mgcv")}
smooth <- run_dose_response_gam(y, exposure = "caffeine",
    celltype = "Monocyte", target_genes = interferon[1:4])
smooth[, c("gene", "edf", "p_smooth", "p_nonlinear", "R2_loocv_gam")]
```

## Mixtures

`run_sc_mixture()` scores each exposure by its quantile and regresses the
pseudobulk expression of each target gene on the scores; it returns the sum of
the coefficients for each gene and, in the metadata, the relative size of the
coefficients of each exposure. It is a screen, without intervals or tests.
`run_mixture_qgcomp()` fits quantile g-computation [@keil2020] with
`r CRANpkg("qgcomp")` to the mean expression of the target genes and returns an
interval and a p-value for the effect of raising all exposures by one quantile.

```{r mixture}
mixture_of <- c("caffeine", "theobromine", "pfos", "pfoa")
mixture <- run_sc_mixture(y, exposures = mixture_of, celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon, covariates = c("age", "sex_male"))
head(mixture[order(-abs(mixture$mixture_effect)), ], 3)
round(metadata(mixture)$weights, 2)
```

```{r qgcomp, eval=has("qgcomp")}
joint <- run_mixture_qgcomp(y, exposures = mixture_of, celltype = "Monocyte",
    target_genes = interferon, covariates = c("age", "sex_male"))
joint[, c("mixture_effect", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "mixture_pvalue",
    "n_donors")]
```

## Genes and proteins

`run_cell_coupling()` is for data with surface proteins measured in the same
cells, kept as an alternative experiment. Within each donor it computes the
Spearman partial correlation between a gene and a protein across the cells of
one cell type, given the RNA and protein library sizes; a meta-regression
across the donors then asks whether this correlation differs with the
exposure. It takes every gene with every protein; the rows of five genes with
their own proteins are shown.

```{r coupling, eval=has("metafor", "ppcor")}
pairs <- data.frame(
    gene = c("HLA-DRA", "CD36", "ITGAM", "FCGR3A", "CD86"),
    protein = c("HLA-DR", "CD36-1", "CD11B", "CD16", "CD86-1")
)
coupling <- run_cell_coupling(y, genes = pairs$gene,
    proteins = pairs$protein, exposure = "ever_smoker", celltype = "Monocyte",
    min_cells = 14L)
own <- paste(coupling$gene, coupling$protein) %in%
    paste(pairs$gene, pairs$protein)
coupling[own, c("gene", "protein", "n_donors", "mean_r", "beta1", "se1",
    "pval1")]
```

`mean_r` is the mean of the partial correlation over the donors, and `beta1`
the slope, across donors, of its Fisher z on the exposure. The default
`min_cells` is 30 cells per donor; the data have 14 monocytes per donor, too
few for an analysis that is meant to be read.

# Related packages

exposomeSC adds a container for donor-level exposures and analyses that are
specific to exposure studies; for the model fits themselves it calls other
packages. The pseudobulk counts are summed by `r Biocpkg("scrapper")`, and the
models are those of `r Biocpkg("edgeR")`, `r Biocpkg("DESeq2")` and
`r Biocpkg("limma")` with `r Biocpkg("variancePartition")`. The packages below
cover neighbouring ground.

- `r Biocpkg("muscat")` analyses differential states in multi-sample,
  multi-group single-cell data, with pseudobulk and mixed-model methods.
  `run_sc_exwas()` fits a pseudobulk model of the same kind for a donor-level
  exposure that is kept in the object.
- `r Biocpkg("dreamlet")` tests pseudobulk differential expression in complex
  study designs, with the mixed models of variancePartition.
  `method = "voom_dream"` calls variancePartition itself, without a random
  effect; it does not use dreamlet.
- `r Biocpkg("rexposome")` and `r Biocpkg("omicRexposome")` hold exposome data
  and associate them with bulk omic data. `as_scee()` takes the exposures of an
  `ExposomeSet` of rexposome into the container.
- `r Biocpkg("speckle")`, `r Biocpkg("crumblr")` and `r Biocpkg("sccomp")` test
  differences in the composition of cell types, as
  `run_exposure_composition()` does; its help page describes how it differs
  from each.

A study whose question is a comparison of groups of samples, without exposure
measurements to keep with the cells, is served by the first two packages
directly.
